record.ear: Fair and cold. High 36. Low 22 at the Whitestone ice house; Sound ice three inches in the coves.

lead.headline: Board hears Mr. Pruitt in private for 95 minutes; record stays sealed
lead.deck: Clerk's counsel asks that the counting-room record be played in his presence; Chairman Delaney takes the request 'under advisement'
lead.body: Mr. Walter Pruitt, receiving clerk at the Jamaica office, was heard by the Board of Elections from 10 a.m. until 11:35 yesterday in Room 14, with his counsel, Mr. Francis Gorman. Mr. Gorman said afterwards that his client had repeated his sworn statement and asked that the sealed record of the night of the 6th be played in his presence. Chairman Delaney said the Board had taken the request under advisement and would state its position on Monday. Mr. Pruitt returned to his desk at 1 p.m.

columns.headline: Queens Light & Power to open its load books to the borough engineer
columns.body: The utility told the Hum committee by letter yesterday that Mr. Oskar Lind, borough engineer, may inspect the Astoria load books at its Vernon Boulevard office from Monday. The books run to fourteen volumes since September. The company repeats that they show no change.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships 2,600 miles south; a dog lost over the side, recovered
columns.body: The Bay Shore station heard the City of New York at 3:31 a.m. in the thirty-fifth degree of south latitude. One dog went over the side in a swell on Wednesday and was recovered by boat in eleven minutes. Commander Byrd names the dog as Nome.

columns.headline: Newtown and Bryant to meet at Dutch Kills tomorrow at 2; record to be kept
columns.body: The high schools of Newtown and Bryant play their annual game at the Dutch Kills ground tomorrow at 2 p.m. The Board of Education has asked that the field system record the game 'for the settlement of disputes.' Newtown has won three years running. Admission 25 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Transit Commission has received the Interborough's letter on Sunday service. It is two lines long.

speaker.ear: Cold and bright. High 36. Three inches in the coves and one on our office window.

lead.headline: Pruitt holds the line for ninety-five minutes; Board keeps him on hold
lead.deck: Clerk tells his story to a shut door; asks to hear the record; Chairman Delaney will think about it until Monday
lead.body: Mr. Pruitt went into Room 14 at ten with a lawyer and came out at twenty-five to twelve with the same lawyer and the same story, which is more than the Board can say for its ledger. He asked to hear the counting-room record with his own ears. The Board has taken this 'under advisement,' which is where it keeps everything it does not want to say out loud. Monday, it promises. We have heard Monday promised before, by the ice men. The Sound froze first.

columns.headline: Utility opens its books to the engineer; the books say what the utility says
columns.body: Queens Light & Power will let Mr. Lind read fourteen volumes of load figures from Monday, all of which show no change, as the company has been saying since September in a voice of no change. Mr. Lind is bringing his own meter. We suggest he bring his own chair.

columns.headline: Byrd's dog goes overboard and comes back on the line
columns.body: A dog named Nome went over the side of the City of New York in a swell and was back aboard in eleven minutes, which is faster than the Board of Elections has moved on anything. Commander Byrd gave the dog's name before the coal. We call that progress.

columns.headline: Newtown versus Bryant tomorrow, and the field will be listening
columns.body: The two high schools meet at Dutch Kills at two, and the Board of Education has ordered the ground to record the game so that disputes may be settled. Disputes at Newtown-Bryant are settled on Vernon Boulevard afterwards. The record is admissible. The bruises already are.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Interborough has written two lines to the Transit Commission. One of them is 'Yours faithfully.'

record.ear: Clear and very cold. High 31. Low 19 at 6 a.m., the first hard frost of the season.

lead.headline: First hard frost: 19 degrees at dawn; 340 burst pipes reported by noon
lead.deck: Insurance adjusters play house records to fix the hour of each burst; plumbers' union asks for a sixteen-hour day
lead.body: The thermometer at the Long Island City courthouse read 19 degrees at 6 a.m. yesterday, the lowest since March 2, and the borough's plumbers answered 340 calls for burst pipes before noon. The Queens Mutual and three other insurers sent adjusters with portable receivers to play back each building's record and fix the hour of the burst, the policies paying only for bursts after midnight. The plumbers' union has asked for a sixteen-hour day until Tuesday. Coal advanced 25 cents to 14 dollars 75.

columns.headline: Week's count: Queens exchange put through 2,204,116 calls; 61 misconnections
columns.body: The Queens exchange reports 2,204,116 connections for the week ending Friday, against 2,131,400 last week, the increase laid to the cold and the count. Operators entered 61 misconnections, 14 of them to the Arcade luncheonette. The longest hold was 41 minutes, to the Board of Elections.

columns.headline: Mr. Pruitt's counsel petitions Supreme Court to compel production of the record
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman filed at the Queens County courthouse at 3:40 p.m. yesterday for an order compelling the Board of Elections to produce the sealed counting-room record for inspection in chambers. The petition is returnable before Justice Thaddeus Rourke on Tuesday at 10.

columns.headline: Third coin box granted; to be bolted to the Arcade wall by Thursday
columns.body: The Borough granted News & Cigars its third kerb coin box yesterday on condition that it be emptied before 7 a.m. and after 6 p.m. and 'make no sound in operation.' The box, of pressed steel and Bakelite, takes cents only. It goes up on Thursday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Newtown and Bryant play at 2 today. The field record will be kept by the Board of Education.

speaker.ear: Nineteen degrees at dawn, and the hum did not shiver once. High 31.

lead.headline: Frost freezes the pipes, and the walls remember exactly when
lead.deck: Three hundred and forty bursts by noon; the adjusters bring their receivers and your cellar testifies against you
lead.body: Nineteen degrees this morning, and every pipe in Queens that was thinking about it went ahead. Three hundred and forty by lunch. The plumbers want a sixteen-hour day and will get it, because nobody else can hold a wrench in this. The adjusters arrived with receivers and played the cellars back, since the policy pays only for bursts after midnight and the cellars know the hour. One householder in Ravenswood was heard at 11:52 saying it would hold. It did not. He is not covered.

columns.headline: Two million calls this week and sixty-one of them got the luncheonette
columns.body: The exchange put through 2,204,116 calls, which is more than the borough has people, so some of you are talking to yourselves. Sixty-one went wrong, fourteen to the luncheonette, Queens's favourite wrong number. The longest hold was 41 minutes, to the Board. It was us.

columns.headline: Pruitt takes the Board to court; wants the record played where a judge can hear
columns.body: Mr. Gorman walked into the courthouse at twenty to four and asked Justice Rourke to make the Board produce the sealed record, in chambers, Tuesday at ten. Chambers have doors too, but a judge's door opens from the inside.

columns.headline: Third box coming Thursday; must be quiet, which is more than they ask of us
columns.body: The Borough says News & Cigars may have a third coin box so long as it makes no sound in operation. A coin box that makes no sound takes no coins. We shall see. It is pressed steel and Bakelite, so it will outlive the Board of Elections.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Newtown-Bryant at two. The field is recording. So is every mother in the stand.

editorial.headline: Doyle resigns for his health; ours is failing too
editorial.body: Alderman Doyle has resigned to rest his nerves, and who could blame him. One week ago he was a public servant; today he is a gramophone. This paper asks the obvious question nobody else will ring up: what decent woman climbs a bank front in the dark? Our mailbag is heavy with letters from the borough's ladies, many of them typed on office machines in office hours, praising this Lilith for 'returning the ice money to the people.' We print none of them. A lady who wants her letters printed should first learn to write to her husband. We propose a modest curfew: no woman abroad after nine without a male relation. The ladies' clubs call this an outrage. The ladies' clubs, we note, meet after nine.

record.ear: Fair, less cold. High 38. Skim ice on the Sound from Whitestone to the Throgs Neck light.

lead.headline: Newtown defeats Bryant 7 to 6; disputed point settled by the field record
lead.deck: Bryant's kick ruled wide after the ground's system is played back to both coaches; 4,200 attend in 31 degrees
lead.body: Newtown High School beat Bryant 7 to 6 at the Dutch Kills ground yesterday before 4,200, its fourth victory in the series. Bryant scored first in the second quarter; its kick for the point was ruled wide by Referee Hanlon. Bryant protested, and at the half the ground's record was played back to both coaches. It contains the crowd and the whistle but not the ball. Mr. Hanlon's ruling stood. Newtown scored in the fourth quarter from the two-yard line and kicked the point.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships in heavy weather at 40 south; dogs below; message brief
columns.body: The City of New York was heard at 2:58 a.m. in a westerly gale at the fortieth parallel, shipping green water. The dogs are below. The message ran ninety seconds and was not played to the press, the Navy saying it concerned the ships' working only.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society asks the borough to record 'one ordinary Sunday' for 1978
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens, at its monthly meeting in Jamaica, resolved to ask every member to record one ordinary Sunday in December in full, to be sealed at Borough Hall for playing in 1978. The Society has 212 members. The secretary asks that members not sing.

columns.headline: Sound sets from Whitestone to the light; Bowery Bay company marks out its field
columns.body: Skim ice ran unbroken from the Whitestone house to the Throgs Neck light at dawn yesterday. The Bowery Bay Ice Company marked out a cutting field of eleven acres with stakes and lanterns. The ice bore a man at the edge by evening. A horse goes on Wednesday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The elevated at Queensboro Plaza did not stop this morning. It stops from December 2.

speaker.ear: Milder. High 38. The Sound has a skin on it and so, after yesterday, has Bryant.

lead.headline: Bryant's point goes wide, and the ground backs the referee
lead.deck: Newtown 7, Bryant 6, and the first high-school point in history lost on the record; the ball, as usual, said nothing
lead.body: Bryant kicked for the point in the second quarter and Referee Hanlon said wide. Bryant said no. The Board of Education said play the ground. So at the half both coaches stood in the groundsman's hut and listened to Dutch Kills, which contains four thousand people shouting, one whistle, and no ball whatever, because a football over a crossbar makes no sound, a fact the Board may now enter in its minutes. Mr. Hanlon's call stood on the record saying nothing against it. Newtown won in the fourth.

columns.headline: Byrd hits a gale at forty south and the Navy hangs up on us
columns.body: The City of New York is shipping green water at forty south and the dogs have gone below, which shows judgment. Commander Byrd's ninety seconds were about the ships' working, so the Navy would not play them, the first message we were not allowed to hear. Not even coal.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a Sunday for 1978, and please do not sing
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society wants its members to record one whole ordinary Sunday for 1978, and the secretary has asked them not to sing. The Lady attended from the corridor. Two hundred and twelve members, and the loudest thing in the room was the resolution. Nineteen seventy-eight gets the radiator.

columns.headline: The Sound sets; the ice men stake their claim and wait for a horse
columns.body: Skim ice from Whitestone to the light, eleven acres staked with lanterns, and a man stood on the edge without going through, which the Bowery Bay company calls a trial and we call a wager. A horse goes on Wednesday. If it has an opinion, Tuesday.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The elevated did not stop at the Plaza this morning. It has two Sundays left to practise.

record.ear: Cloudy, wind east. High 40. Snow possible by Wednesday.

lead.headline: Elevated train stalls on the Plaza approach; 1,100 held 48 minutes in the cold
lead.deck: Motor truck failure at 7:52 a.m.; passengers walked along the structure to the platform; Interborough lays it to a frozen contact
lead.body: A six-car train of the Astoria line stalled on the curved approach to Queensboro Plaza at 7:52 yesterday morning with about 1,100 passengers aboard and stood 48 minutes in 28 degrees. The Interborough says the trailing motor truck lost its contact shoe to ice on the third rail. At 8:40 the guards walked the passengers along the structure to the platform, two abreast. No one was hurt. The train's record was removed by an inspector. The Transit Commission hears the matter on the 27th at 10.

columns.headline: Long Island City Athletic Club defeats Paterson 20 to 0 before 3,400
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club beat the Paterson Silk Sox 20 to 0 at Dutch Kills yesterday on a frozen ground. Two of the three touchdowns followed fumbles. Referee Collins reported no disturbance from Jackson Avenue receivers, the householder of last week having been spoken to.

columns.headline: Landlords' association objects to Listening Act fee; calls it 'a tax on walls'
columns.body: The Queens Real Estate Owners' Association resolved on Saturday to oppose Senator Harlan's licence fee of 5 dollars a building, which its president, Mr. Ambrose Tully, called 'a tax on walls that were listening before there was a Senator.' It does not oppose the admission of records in evidence.

columns.headline: Valves 6 for 97 cents; eggs 63; the Newark works on a night shift
columns.body: The Arcade hardware counter raised the six-sleeve of receiving valves a cent to 97 yesterday, the Newark works having put on a night shift for the cold-weather demand. Eggs are 63 cents the dozen. Coal holds at 14 dollars 75.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board of Elections will state its position on Mr. Pruitt's request at 11 a.m. today.

speaker.ear: Grey and raw. High 40. The elevated is running, which is news.

lead.headline: Eleven hundred put on hold at the Plaza, forty-eight minutes, no music
lead.deck: Third-rail shoe freezes on the curve; passengers walk the structure two by two; the Interborough blames the weather, as it has since 1917
lead.body: At eight minutes to eight the Astoria train stopped on the curve into Queensboro Plaza and stayed there forty-eight minutes with eleven hundred people in it and no heat, the Interborough's idea of a connection. A shoe froze, they say. Everybody's shoes froze. At twenty to nine the guards walked the whole train along the structure two by two, forty feet over Jackson Avenue, and nobody fell, because nobody could feel their feet. The train's record holds forty-eight minutes of opinions. The commission plays it on the 27th.

columns.headline: Athletic Club shuts out Paterson, and the receivers on Jackson Avenue shut up
columns.body: Twenty to nothing on a skating rink, two of the scores on fumbles, which in this cold is a strategy. The householder who played his receiver at the referee last week was 'spoken to' by the club secretary and has gone quiet. We know what the secretary weighs.

columns.headline: Landlords say the Listening Act is a tax on walls; the walls decline to comment
columns.body: Three thousand landlords have decided that five dollars a year is too much for a wall that was already listening for nothing. They do not object to the records going to court; only to paying for it. It is the first time a Queens landlord has defended a tenant's wall.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why is my valve a cent dearer than Saturday?'
columns.body: Sir, because Newark has gone on nights, and a man who works nights wants paying, and the sleeve goes through four hands before yours. Ninety-seven cents. Eggs are up too and nobody writes in about hens. Buy on Monday; by Friday the counterman will have read another thermometer.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board speaks at eleven on Mr. Pruitt. We have a man in the corridor and a man in the safe. Joking about the safe.

record.ear: Cloudy, cold. High 37. The Weather Bureau expects snow tomorrow afternoon.

lead.headline: Board refuses Mr. Pruitt the record; Justice Rourke hears petition at 10 today
lead.deck: Chairman Delaney: the record 'is the Board's and will be opened by the Board or by a court, not by a clerk'; Mr. Gorman says the court will do
lead.body: The Board of Elections announced at 11:04 yesterday that it would not play the sealed record of the counting room to Mr. Walter Pruitt or his counsel. Chairman Delaney read a statement of 94 words, which said that the record 'is the Board's and will be opened by the Board or by a court, not by a clerk.' Mr. Francis Gorman, for Mr. Pruitt, said the court would do; his petition is returnable before Justice Rourke at 10 this morning.

columns.headline: Borough engineer's own meter reads 41 cycles in four Astoria cellars
columns.body: Mr. Oskar Lind, before opening the utility's load books, spent yesterday morning in four cellars on Steinway Street with a frequency meter of his own and read a tone of 41 cycles in each. He declines to say what it is. The utility says its plant turns at 60 cycles.

columns.headline: Astoria boy, 11, reports WORS 1610 on a crystal set; Radio Division sends a man
columns.body: A boy of eleven on 31st Street told the Queens exchange on Sunday night that his crystal set, which has no valve, had received a station announcing itself as WORS 1610 at 9:20 p.m. for a minute. The Radio Division's inspector heard nothing and has borrowed the set.

columns.headline: Turkeys 47 cents the pound at Dutch Kills market; 2,000 charity dinners planned
columns.body: Dressed turkeys are 47 cents the pound at Dutch Kills market, up 3 on last year. The Salvation Army and the Legion post will serve 2,000 Thanksgiving dinners on the 29th at the Vernon Boulevard hall from noon. The Mayor's proclamation will be read at 11:45 and recorded.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships out of the gale at 3:15 a.m. Dogs on deck. Coal within estimate.

speaker.ear: Snow coming, the Bureau says. High 37. The hum is 41 in four cellars, same as our office.

lead.headline: Board hangs up on Pruitt; the court picks up at ten
lead.deck: Ninety-four words from Chairman Delaney: the record belongs to the Board, or a judge, but never a clerk; Mr. Gorman says a judge will do nicely
lead.body: Chairman Delaney read ninety-four words yesterday at four minutes past eleven, and we counted every one. The record is the Board's. It may be opened by the Board, which will not, or by a court, which may, but never by a clerk, which is odd, because a clerk made it. Mr. Gorman thanked the chairman and said see you at ten. The Board has hired Mr. Hiram Voss, who has never lost a case the Board wanted won. Mr. Pruitt sat at his desk throughout, receiving.

columns.headline: Engineer finds the hum in four cellars; utility says it cannot count that low
columns.body: Mr. Lind carried his own meter down four Steinway Street cellars and got 41 cycles four times, the hum's number, which every Astorian knows the way they know their rent. He will not say what it is. Queens Light & Power says its plant turns at 60. Nobody asked the plant.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? An eleven-year-old gets it on a cat's whisker and no valve
columns.body: A boy on 31st Street heard WORS 1610 for a minute Sunday night on a crystal set, which has no valve, no battery and no business receiving after dark. The Division sent a man who heard nothing and borrowed the set, the first sighting it thought worth taking.

columns.headline: Turkey's up three cents; the Mayor's proclamation to be recorded for the Mayor
columns.body: Forty-seven cents a pound dressed, and if you want it undressed, see the Lady. The Legion and the Army feed two thousand on the 29th, and the Mayor's proclamation will be recorded so the Mayor can hear how it went. It went well. They always do.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd is out of the gale and the dogs are back on deck. The coal is fine. Thank you for asking.

record.ear: Snow beginning by afternoon, two inches expected. High 33.

lead.headline: Ice company horse walks seven miles from Whitestone to his old stable
lead.deck: Dutchman, a Percheron of 1,900 pounds, left the Whitestone house at 5 a.m. and was found at 7:40 at the door of the Vernon Avenue yard he left in 1925
lead.body: A grey Percheron gelding named Dutchman, bought by the Bowery Bay Ice Company on Monday, let himself out of the Whitestone stable at about 5 a.m. yesterday and walked to the Vernon Avenue coal yard in Dutch Kills, where he worked until 1925. The yard foreman, Mr. Anton Keller, found him at the gate at 7:40 and telephoned the exchange. The bridge keeper says he crossed 'on the right side.' Dutchman was returned by van and is to be tried on the ice today.

columns.headline: Justice Rourke orders Board to produce sealed record in chambers Friday at 10
columns.body: Justice Rourke ruled at 11:50 yesterday that the Board of Elections must produce the counting-room record in his chambers on Friday at 10, to be played once before counsel and Mr. Pruitt. Mr. Voss, for the Board, asked for a week and was given three days.

columns.headline: Arcade luncheonette's booth telephone connected; first call was to the counter
columns.body: The Queens exchange connected the Vantry Arcade luncheonette's second instrument, in a booth by the door, at 9:15 yesterday, a day late. The first call from the booth, at 9:17, was to the counter, eleven feet away, by the proprietor, 'to see that it worked.' It worked.

columns.headline: Transit Commission staff hear the stalled train's record; passengers invited
columns.body: The commission's engineers played the record of Sunday's stalled Astoria train in private yesterday and found it 'complete.' It runs 51 minutes. Passengers who wish to be heard at the hearing of the 27th may give their names at Borough Hall. Fourteen had done so by 5 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships 600 miles from New Zealand in fair weather. Coal within estimate.

speaker.ear: Snow on the way. High 33. Dutchman knew the road; the Weather Bureau only knows the forecast.

lead.headline: Horse hangs up on Whitestone, calls at his old number
lead.deck: Dutchman, nineteen hundred pounds of opinion, walks seven miles home to Dutch Kills before breakfast; the ice men came for him by trolley
lead.body: The Bowery Bay company bought a horse on Monday and lost him on Tuesday. Dutchman let himself out at five and walked to the Vernon Avenue coal yard, where he worked three years ago and where, in his view, he still does. He crossed the Flushing bridge on the right side, which is more than the ice vans manage. Mr. Keller found him at the gate at twenty to eight, waiting to be let in. He goes on the Sound today. We give it till Thursday.

columns.headline: Judge gives the Board three days to bring the record; it asked for a week
columns.body: Justice Rourke says Friday at ten, in chambers, the record played once to the lawyers and to Mr. Pruitt, who made it. Mr. Voss asked for a week and got three days, the first time anybody got less time than they wanted. We shall be in the corridor.

columns.headline: Booth telephone lands at the luncheonette; proprietor rings himself to check
columns.body: The second instrument went in at a quarter past nine, and at seventeen minutes past the proprietor stood in the booth and rang his own counter, eleven feet off, to see that it worked. It did. The counter answered. We are told the conversation was short and about the coffee.

columns.headline: Fourteen passengers volunteer to be heard about the train they were heard on
columns.body: The Transit Commission has played the stalled train's record in private, fifty-one minutes of it, and calls it complete. We expect it is. Fourteen passengers have signed up for the 27th, so the commission will hear them twice, once in person and once in the record, saying worse.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd is 600 miles off New Zealand. The dogs can smell sheep.

record.ear: Snow ended, 2 inches. Fair and cold. High 34. Roads slow on the hills.

lead.headline: Alderman Feeney's daughter married at St. Mary's; groom a utility line foreman
lead.deck: Miss Margaret Feeney weds Mr. Thomas Carew at 11; the Alderman says his place on the Hum committee is 'not affected'
lead.body: Miss Margaret Feeney, 23, daughter of Alderman and Mrs. Patrick Feeney of Hunters Point, was married at 11 a.m. yesterday at St. Mary's to Mr. Thomas Carew, 27, a line foreman of Queens Light & Power. Father Dunne officiated. The parish record was taken at the family's request. Asked whether the marriage bore on his seat on the committee that hears the Astoria petition on Tuesday, the Alderman said it was 'not affected,' and that his son-in-law 'strings wire and has no opinion on cycles.'

columns.headline: Senator Harlan says Listening Act fee 'may be 3 dollars'; landlords unmoved
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan told the Record by telephone yesterday that the licence fee in his draft 'may be 3 dollars rather than 5' when the Judiciary Committee sits in January. Mr. Ambrose Tully, for the real estate owners, said the association objected 'to the principle, not the figure.'

columns.headline: Dutchman tried on the Sound ice; bears him at four inches; cutting Saturday
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company walked the Percheron Dutchman onto the cove ice at Whitestone at 10 a.m. yesterday with a man at his head. The ice, four inches, bore him for 200 yards. Cutting begins Saturday with 140 men. Dutchman was stabled with the door chained.

columns.headline: Third coin box bolted to the Arcade wall; made no sound in a trial of 50 cents
columns.body: The ironmonger fitted News & Cigars' third kerb box at 2 p.m. yesterday and tried it with fifty cents before a Borough inspector, who entered it as 'silent in operation.' It takes the Record at 6 a.m. and the Speaker at 5 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board of Elections has removed the sealed record from its safe to the Justice's chambers under escort.

speaker.ear: Two inches, and quiet under it. High 34. The hum does not take snow days.

lead.headline: Alderman's daughter marries into the load books
lead.deck: Miss Feeney weds a Queens Light & Power lineman at St. Mary's; father says the committee is not affected, and the groom has no opinion on cycles
lead.body: The Alderman who sits in judgment on the hum on Tuesday gave his daughter away to a man who strings wire for the company that denies it. We merely report that the parish kept the record at the family's request, and nowhere in it does anybody say 41. The Alderman says his son-in-law has no opinion on cycles, the only man in Astoria without one. The Lady says the bride wore ivory and the groom wore the expression of a man who has met the Alderman.

columns.headline: Harlan knocks two dollars off the walls; landlords object on principle
columns.body: Five dollars may be three dollars by January, the Senator says, having heard from three thousand landlords. Mr. Tully says the association objects to the principle, not the figure. That is what a man says when the figure has come down and he would like it to keep going.

columns.headline: Dutchman takes the ice, two hundred yards, and does not go home
columns.body: The horse that walked to Dutch Kills on Tuesday walked on the Sound on Wednesday with a man at his head and four inches under him, and stayed. Two hundred yards. Cutting starts Saturday. They have chained the stable door, which holds until he learns chains. A week.

columns.headline: Third box goes up and says nothing, the first silent thing on Jackson Avenue
columns.body: Fifty cents went through it in front of an inspector and the box never made a sound, so it is now the quietest object on the avenue, and holds us from five. The other two are to be oiled. A third box shamed them.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The sealed record went from the safe to the judge's chambers under escort. Two policemen and a clerk. Not that clerk.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 35. Low 21. Cutting on the Sound begins tomorrow.

lead.headline: Record played in chambers: Riverhead heard twice, second voice unknown
lead.deck: Justice Rourke: the record carries a wire reception at 9:48 and a telephone entry at 10:31 'in another voice'; ledger sent to a handwriting examiner; hearing December 3
lead.body: The sealed counting-room record was played in Justice Rourke's chambers from 10:06 to 11:40 yesterday before counsel and Mr. Walter Pruitt. The Justice said afterwards that the record carries the Riverhead returns received by wire at 9:48 p.m., in a voice counsel agree is Mr. Pruitt's, and again by telephone at 10:31 'in another voice, not identified.' The ledger has gone to a handwriting examiner. The Board is to name every person in the room at 10:31. Adjourned to December 3.

columns.headline: Dutchman to stay at Dutch Kills; coal yard buys him back for the winter
columns.body: Mr. Anton Keller, foreman of the Vernon Avenue coal yard, bought the Percheron Dutchman back from the Bowery Bay Ice Company yesterday for 210 dollars, the company having concluded that 'the horse has made his position clear.' He hauls coal from Monday. The company will hire another horse.

columns.headline: Bryant High protests Saturday's point to the Board of Education
columns.body: Bryant High School filed a protest with the Board of Education yesterday against Referee Hanlon's ruling of Saturday and asked that the Dutch Kills ground record be played before the full Board. The Board will consider the request on Monday. Newtown's principal said the record 'contains no ball.'

columns.headline: Byrd's ships to make Dunedin on Monday; dogs to be landed first
columns.body: The Navy's Bay Shore station heard the City of New York at 4:02 a.m., 300 miles from Dunedin, New Zealand, where the ships will coal. The 95 dogs are to be landed first for exercise. Commander Byrd's message, played in the Record's window at noon, ran four minutes.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board of Elections says it will name those in the room at 10:31 'when it has consulted its own record.'

speaker.ear: Cold and clear. High 35. The record has been played, and the whole borough is holding its breath, badly.

lead.headline: The record speaks: Riverhead rang twice, and the second voice is nobody's
lead.deck: Judge hears the room; Pruitt answered the wire at 9:48; somebody else answered the telephone at 10:31 and has not put their hand up
lead.body: Ninety-four minutes in chambers, and the counting room finally spoke. Mr. Pruitt received Riverhead by wire at 9:48, in his own voice. Then at 10:31 somebody else received Riverhead by telephone, in a voice the Justice calls 'not identified,' the politest name for a stranger we have heard this year. The ledger has gone to a handwriting man. The Board must name everyone in the room at 10:31, once it has consulted its own record. A different one, we assume.

columns.headline: Dutchman wins: the coal yard buys him back and the ice men call it a position
columns.body: Two hundred and ten dollars and the horse is home for good, the ice company having decided that 'the horse has made his position clear,' the most sensible sentence a company has spoken in this borough since September. He hauls coal from Monday. He never wanted the Sound.

columns.headline: Bryant wants the full Board to hear the ball that made no sound
columns.body: Bryant has asked the Board of Education to sit down and listen to Saturday's record, all of it, for a point that was wide or was not. Newtown's principal observes that the record contains no ball. The Board considers it Monday. We suggest the sound down, which will be quicker.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Nowhere this week, and the boy wants his set back
columns.body: No sightings since Sunday, and the eleven-year-old on 31st Street has written to the Radio Division asking for his crystal set back, as he has homework. The Division has it in a drawer, listening. It has heard nothing. The boy heard a minute.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board will name the room at 10:31 'when it has consulted its own record.' It has one of those too.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 36. Four and a half inches of ice at Whitestone; cutting begins at 7.

lead.headline: 61 ask to be heard on the Hum; committee allows five minutes each and one meter
lead.deck: Tuesday's hearing to run from 2 p.m.; Queens Light & Power to open; Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia to bring a frequency meter and a witness who 'cannot hear it'
lead.body: The committee of Alderman Feeney, Dr. Ruth Albrecht and Mr. Oskar Lind announced yesterday that 61 persons have asked to be heard at Tuesday's hearing on the Astoria petition, each for five minutes from 2 p.m. Queens Light & Power will open with its load books. Dr. Emil Rastin of Columbia will bring a frequency meter and 'a witness who cannot hear it,' a Mrs. Oda of Steinway Street. The committee sits in the Borough Hall chamber, whose own record will be kept.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,106 burst pipes since the 16th; insurers paid on 740
columns.body: The borough's plumbers report 1,106 burst pipes between the frost of the 16th and last night, and the Queens Mutual and three other insurers report payment on 740 of them after playing the house records. Three hundred and sixty-six bursts fell before midnight. Two adjusters have resigned.

columns.headline: Ice cutting begins at Whitestone today; 140 men, five horses
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company cuts its first Sound ice at 7 this morning on the eleven-acre field off Whitestone, with 140 men, five horses and a sixth 'engaged.' The ice measured four and a half inches at dawn. The company expects 300 tons by dark.

columns.headline: Comptroller's list: Jackson Avenue's 38 lamps set in one afternoon, October 18
columns.body: The Comptroller's autumn list of street work shows 38 lamp standards set on Jackson Avenue on October 18 between noon and 5 p.m. The 4,180 dollars voted for them in 1925 and 'not since located' was located on October 17, the Comptroller's office states. The work had been estimated for 1931.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board of Elections has given Justice Rourke a list of nine names for 10:31 on the 6th. It is sealed.

speaker.ear: Cold and fair. High 36. Four and a half inches, and the ice men are finally cutting something besides excuses.

lead.headline: Sixty-one want five minutes with the hum; the hum wants nothing from anyone
lead.deck: Tuesday at two, Borough Hall, and the chamber will record the hearing about a tone it has been recording since September
lead.body: Sixty-one Astorians have asked to speak on Tuesday and the committee will give them five minutes each, which is 305 minutes of complaint, a borough record. Queens Light & Power goes first with fourteen volumes of no change. Then Dr. Rastin of Columbia with a meter and a woman from Steinway Street who cannot hear it, the first witness in history called for not hearing something. The chamber will take its own record as a matter of course. It has been humming at 41 since September like everything else.

columns.headline: Eleven hundred pipes, seven hundred paid, two adjusters gone
columns.body: A week of frost: 1,106 bursts, 740 of them paid, 366 of them before midnight and therefore your own fault, says the policy. Two adjusters have resigned after eight days of playing cellars back and hearing householders say it would hold. The cellars never lie.

columns.headline: Ice men cut at last; five horses and a sixth 'engaged,' which is not Dutchman
columns.body: Seven this morning, 140 men on the Sound and five horses, with a sixth engaged, and we have it on authority that the sixth was asked whether he had ever worked in Dutch Kills. The ice is four and a half inches. The company wants 300 tons by dark.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the Thanksgiving game be on the wire?'
columns.body: Madam, the Dutch Kills ground records; it does not broadcast, and if it did you would hear four thousand people and a whistle and never the ball. Go. Wear two coats. Keep off the lines, the Board says, meaning the chalk ones. The other lines keep themselves.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nine names in the room at 10:31, sealed. The Board seals faster than the Sound.

editorial.headline: Thanksgiving thief turns turkey into a turkey trot
editorial.body: Forty-one widows of the Astoria ice routes found envelopes under their doors this week, each tied with a black silk bow, each holding exactly the sum Alderman Doyle's contractors had overcharged them since 1926, to the cent, with a card: Pay no man twice. Our readers call it charity. We call it receiving. Where did the money come from? From the Alderman's safe, which was found open and polished, with a lipstick spider drawn on the mirror above it. A man's safe is the last private room left to him. If a woman may open it because she disapproves of what is inside, then no man in Queens is safe in his own safe. Give thanks, widows. Then give it back.

record.ear: Snow overnight, three inches. Clearing. High 32. Trolleys running late on Vernon Boulevard.

lead.headline: Three inches of snow; quietest night on the exchange since 1924, 61,400 calls
lead.deck: Operators report the borough 'audibly still' between 1 and 5 a.m.; the only sustained traffic was to the ice house and the Record
lead.body: Three inches of snow fell on the borough between 9 last night and 3 this morning, and the Queens exchange reports the quietest night since the storm of February 1924: 61,400 calls between midnight and 6, against a usual 140,000. The night supervisor, Miss Agnes Pohl, entered the borough as 'audibly still' between 1 and 5. The only sustained traffic was to the Whitestone ice house, which cut 290 tons yesterday and kept a watchman on the field, and to this office.

columns.headline: Byrd's ships 90 miles from Dunedin; harbour pilot to meet them at dawn Monday
columns.body: The Navy's Bay Shore station heard the City of New York at 3:48 a.m. 90 miles off Dunedin, running in fine weather with the Eleanor Bolling in company. The harbour pilot meets them at dawn Monday, New Zealand time. The dogs will be landed on the breakwater.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society's 'ordinary Sunday' to be recorded next week; 180 pledged
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society reports that 180 of its 212 members have pledged to record Sunday December 2 in full, from waking to sleep, for sealing at Borough Hall. The secretary reminds members that the day must be ordinary and asks that no member invite guests 'for the record.'

columns.headline: Elevated makes a trial stop at Queensboro Plaza at 10:05; 14 passengers get off
columns.body: The Interborough stopped a Sunday morning Astoria train at Queensboro Plaza at 10:05 yesterday as a trial of the service that begins December 2. Fourteen passengers alighted and nine boarded. The stop ran 40 seconds. The Transit Commission's observer entered the train as 'quieter when stopped.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power has delivered fourteen volumes to Borough Hall for Tuesday. They were brought by van.

speaker.ear: Three inches, and the hum under it like a cat under a quilt. High 32.

lead.headline: Snow puts the borough on mute; sixty-one thousand people still talking
lead.deck: Quietest night since 1924, says the exchange, which means a mere ten calls a second; the ice house and this paper kept the lines warm
lead.body: It snowed, and Queens shut up, by its own standards. Sixty-one thousand calls between midnight and six, against the usual hundred and forty, and the night supervisor wrote 'audibly still' in the book, the nicest thing the exchange has ever said about us. Who was talking? The ice house, which cut 290 tons yesterday and had a man on the field all night counting them. And this office, which was talking to the ice house. The borough slept. The hum did not, and we had the window open.

columns.headline: Byrd ninety miles out and the dogs get the breakwater; coal gets a rest
columns.body: The City of New York makes Dunedin at dawn Monday, their time, and the first thing ashore will be ninety-five dogs on a breakwater, which New Zealand has not been warned about. The coal is within estimate for the twenty-third time. We believe him.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a hundred and eighty ordinary Sundays, no guests, please
columns.body: The Society will record next Sunday from waking to sleep and seal it for 1978, and the secretary asks that no member invite guests for the record. The Lady has seen the membership. Nobody was going to. Nineteen seventy-eight will hear a hundred and eighty people being careful.

columns.headline: Elevated stops at the Plaza for forty seconds and is 'quieter when stopped'
columns.body: A trial stop at 10:05, fourteen off, nine on, forty seconds, and the commission's observer wrote that the train was quieter when stopped, a finding that cost the Interborough eleven years and the Mayor a circular. From December 2 it stops every Sunday morning. Weekdays, it keeps its opinion.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Fourteen volumes of no change arrived at Borough Hall by van. The van made more noise.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 34. Snow lying on the north side of the streets.

lead.headline: Byrd's ships reach Dunedin; 95 dogs landed; message played to 300 in the snow
lead.deck: City of New York and Eleanor Bolling moored at 6:40 a.m. New Zealand time; Commander Byrd's message heard in the Record's window at 2:15 yesterday
lead.body: The City of New York and the Eleanor Bolling moored at Dunedin, New Zealand, at 6:40 yesterday morning, local time, thirty-seven days out of Norfolk. The 95 dogs were landed on the breakwater before the mails. Commander Byrd's message was played in the Record's window at 2:15 p.m. to about 300 persons in the snow. It ran six minutes, named the harbour pilot, and reported the pup Bay Shore 'in health and ashore.' The ships sail for the ice on December 2.

columns.headline: Athletic Club and Hoboken play to no score on snow; 1,900 attend
columns.body: The Long Island City Athletic Club and the Hoboken Rovers played to no score at Dutch Kills yesterday on three inches of snow, swept from the lines only. Referee Collins stopped play twice for the ball to be found. The ground's record, the club says, 'contains mostly weather.'

columns.headline: Board of Education hears Bryant's protest today; ground record played at 4
columns.body: The Board of Education will play the Dutch Kills ground record of the 17th at 4 p.m. today in the Jamaica office before deciding Bryant High School's protest against Referee Hanlon's ruling. Both principals will attend. The record runs two hours; the Board will hear the second quarter only.

columns.headline: Valves 6 for 98 cents, up 1; eggs 64; turkeys 48 cents the pound
columns.body: The Arcade hardware counter lists the six-sleeve at 98 cents, up a cent since Monday last. Eggs are 64 cents the dozen at Dutch Kills market and dressed turkeys 48 cents the pound. Coal holds at 14 dollars 75. The counterman expects the dollar sleeve by Christmas.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power will be represented at tomorrow's hearing by its chief engineer and two clerks carrying the books.

speaker.ear: Cold and fair. High 34. The snow has gone grey, which is how Queens says it is Monday.

lead.headline: Byrd reaches Dunedin; ninety-five dogs off the hook
lead.deck: Thirty-seven days, one gale, one dog overboard and a pup born at sea; New Zealand gets the dogs before the mail and the Record's window gets the message
lead.body: They made it. Thirty-seven days out of Norfolk and the dogs went ashore before the letters did, which tells you whose voyage it was. Three hundred people stood in the snow on Jackson Avenue yesterday to hear six minutes of Commander Byrd, and he named the harbour pilot before he named the coal. Bay Shore the pup is ashore and in health. The ships leave for the ice on the 2nd, the Sunday the elevated starts stopping at the Plaza. Two improvements, one day.

columns.headline: Nil-nil in the snow, and the record contains mostly weather
columns.body: The Athletic Club and Hoboken played ninety minutes on three inches of snow yesterday and between them produced no score and two lost balls. Referee Collins stopped play to hunt for the ball, which is a first. The club says the ground's record contains mostly weather. So does the ground.

columns.headline: Board of Education to play the second quarter and nothing else, which is wise
columns.body: At four today the Board will sit in Jamaica and listen to the second quarter of the Newtown-Bryant game. They will hear four thousand people and a whistle. They will not hear a ball. Bryant's hopes are pinned on a cough.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who found the lamp money?'
columns.body: Sir, nobody will say. It was lost from 1925 and found on the seventeenth of October, and on the eighteenth Jackson Avenue had thirty-eight lamps by suppertime. It is the fastest thing the Borough has done since the Dutch left. The operator has not been told who asked, and she is told everything.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The utility sends its chief engineer and two clerks to carry the books tomorrow. The books have never needed carrying before.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 35. Borough Hall opens at 9; both hearings are public.

lead.headline: Hum hearing opens at Borough Hall at 2 today; stalled train played at 10
lead.deck: Sixty-one speakers listed for the Astoria petition; fourteen passengers listed for the elevated; the chamber will be in use for nine hours
lead.body: Borough Hall holds two public hearings today. At 10 a.m. the Transit Commission hears the Interborough on the stalling of the Astoria train on the 18th, and will play the train's record of 51 minutes before fourteen passengers. At 2 p.m. the committee of Alderman Feeney, Dr. Ruth Albrecht and Mr. Oskar Lind hears the Astoria petition on the Hum, Queens Light & Power opening with its load books and 61 speakers following at five minutes each. The chamber's own record will be kept throughout.

columns.headline: Board of Education upholds Referee Hanlon; kick 'neither wide nor good'
columns.body: The Board of Education played the second quarter of the record yesterday and found that it 'neither shows the kick wide nor shows it good.' The referee's ruling stands. Bryant's principal said the school 'accepts the record, which is more than the record did for us.'

columns.headline: Senator Harlan fixes January 9 for the Listening Act; fee 'open'
columns.body: Senator Edmund Harlan's office confirmed yesterday that the Judiciary Committee will take up the Listening Act on January 9 at Albany. The Senator will propose the licence fee as 'open,' between 3 and 5 dollars. The real estate owners will send Mr. Ambrose Tully and their own stenographer.

columns.headline: Pup Bay Shore missing 40 minutes at Dunedin; found in a coal lighter
columns.body: A message from Commander Byrd relayed by the Navy at 4:12 a.m. reports that the pup Bay Shore was missing on the Dunedin breakwater for 40 minutes on Sunday and was found asleep in a coal lighter. The dogs are kennelled ashore. The ships coal today.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruitt will attend the Hum hearing as a resident of Astoria. He has not asked to speak.

speaker.ear: Cold and fair. High 35. The hum had its day in court and did not take the stand.

lead.headline: Hum hearing: three hours in, the chamber hums along
lead.deck: Fourteen volumes say no change; Dr. Rastin's meter says 41 in the room itself; Mrs. Oda hears nothing and is believed; adjourned to December 11
lead.body: The utility opened at two with fourteen volumes, all saying no change. At 3:10 Dr. Rastin of Columbia set his meter on the committee table and it read 41, in the chamber, the first time the hum has been seen. Then Mrs. Oda of Steinway Street swore she could not hear it, and was believed by everyone, because she was the only person in the room not listening. The Alderman adjourned at 6:50 to December 11. The chamber's record ran throughout. It hums too.

columns.headline: Commission plays the stalled train in full; passengers hear themselves
columns.body: Fifty-one minutes at ten this morning, the whole train, and fourteen passengers sat and heard what they had said about the Interborough at eight on a Sunday. Two asked for it to be stopped. The company's man said 'weather.' The commission adjourned to consider heaters.

columns.headline: Bryant loses on a record that says nothing either way, a draw in our book
columns.body: The Board of Education listened to thirty-one minutes of second quarter and ruled that the kick was neither wide nor good on the record, so the referee stands. Bryant's principal accepts the record, which did nothing for him. Ask the Board of Elections.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Not at Borough Hall, where everything else in Queens was today
columns.body: A quiet week for the transmitter: no tugs, no boys, and nothing at Borough Hall today, though two speakers mentioned it in their five minutes and were ruled out of order. The Alderman says WORS is not before the committee. Nothing is ever before anyone.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Adjourned to December 11. The books went home by van. The hum went home with everybody.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 36. Thanksgiving tomorrow: fair, high 38, the Bureau says.

lead.headline: Hum committee asks utility to cut the Astoria feeder for ten minutes as a test
lead.deck: Hearing runs 4 hours 50 minutes; load books show no change; Mr. Lind's and Dr. Rastin's meters agree at 41 in the chamber; adjourned to December 11
lead.body: The committee on the Astoria petition adjourned at 6:50 last night to December 11 after hearing Queens Light & Power, Dr. Rastin, Mrs. Oda and 22 of the 61 speakers. The utility's load books show no change since September. Dr. Rastin's meter and Mr. Lind's both read 41 cycles in the chamber. Alderman Feeney asked the company to cut the Astoria feeder for ten minutes on a December night as a test. The chief engineer said the company 'will consider it.'

columns.headline: Transit Commission orders heaters on contact shoes by January 1
columns.body: The Transit Commission ruled yesterday that the Interborough must fit electric heaters to the contact shoes of all Astoria and Corona trains by January 1, following the playing of the stalled train's record. The company said it would comply. The record was returned sealed, at the passengers' request.

columns.headline: Mayor's proclamation to be read at 11:45 tomorrow; 2,000 dinners from noon
columns.body: The Mayor's Thanksgiving proclamation will be read at 11:45 tomorrow at the Vernon Boulevard hall by Alderman Feeney, recorded, and followed from noon by 2,000 dinners served by the Salvation Army and the Legion post. The Record's window will carry the President-elect's message at noon.

columns.headline: Handwriting examiner to report on the ledger by Saturday; nine names sealed
columns.body: Mr. Carl Brandt, the handwriting examiner, told the Record he would report on the counting-room ledger by Saturday. The Board of Elections' sealed list of nine persons present at 10:31 on the 6th remains with the Justice. Mr. Pruitt attended the Hum hearing and did not speak.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power repeats that its load 'has not changed and will not be interrupted for a test without cause.'

speaker.ear: Cold and fair. High 36. Thanksgiving tomorrow, and the hum has nothing to be thankful for.

lead.headline: Pull the switch, says the Alderman; the utility will think about it, lights on
lead.deck: Ten minutes of dark in Astoria would settle the hum one way or the other, and Queens Light & Power would rather not know
lead.body: Four hours and fifty minutes, two meters reading 41 side by side on the table, and at the end of it Alderman Feeney asked the one question worth asking: turn Astoria off for ten minutes one night and let us listen. The chief engineer said the company will consider it. This morning it says the load has not changed and will not be interrupted without cause. A meter on the committee's own table is not cause. We are beginning to think the cause is the point.

columns.headline: Heaters on the shoes by New Year; the elevated to be warm in one place at last
columns.body: The Interborough must put heaters on its contact shoes by January 1, so the one part of the train nobody sits on will be warm. The stalled train's record went back to the company sealed, the first time anyone here has asked for less to be heard.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will my sister in Flushing ring tomorrow?'
columns.body: Madam, the Operator does not know your sister, but she knows Flushing, and Flushing rings at ten past two on Thanksgiving, after the bird and before the argument. Keep the line clear from two. If she has not rung by three she is not ringing.

columns.headline: Handwriting man promises Saturday; the nine names stay in the judge's drawer
columns.body: Mr. Brandt will say by Saturday whose hand wrote Riverhead twice, and the Board's list of the nine in the room at 10:31 stays sealed until December 3. Mr. Pruitt went to the Hum hearing and said nothing, which he is good at. He has had practice.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The utility will not pull the switch 'without cause.' We have 2,318 causes and a meter.

record.ear: Fair and cold. High 38. Thanksgiving Day. The Record publishes; the counting house is closed.

lead.headline: Thanksgiving: Mr. Hoover's message heard from the Maryland; 2,000 to dine
lead.deck: President-elect's message of 212 words received by the Navy at 5:30 a.m. from the Pacific; to be played in the Record's window at noon; Mayor's proclamation at 11:45
lead.body: The borough observes Thanksgiving today. A message from Mr. Hoover, aboard the battleship Maryland, was received by the Navy at 5:30 this morning and will be played in the Record's window at noon. It runs 212 words, on gratitude and the harvest. At 11:45 Alderman Feeney reads the Mayor's proclamation at the Vernon Boulevard hall, where the Salvation Army and the Legion post serve 2,000 dinners from noon. The elevated runs a Sunday service and will stop at Queensboro Plaza.

columns.headline: Newtown plays Flushing at 11, Athletic Club meets Bayonne at 2; both recorded
columns.body: Newtown High School meets Flushing High at the Dutch Kills ground at 11 this morning and the Long Island City Athletic Club meets the Bayonne Pioneers at 2. Both games will be recorded by the ground. Admission 25 cents in the morning and 50 in the afternoon.

columns.headline: Whitestone field closed today; 1,120 tons cut in five days; ice five inches
columns.body: The Bowery Bay Ice Company closes its Whitestone field today for the holiday, having cut 1,120 tons of Sound ice since Saturday with 140 men and six horses. The ice measured five inches yesterday. Cutting resumes tomorrow at 7. No horse has left the field without instruction.

columns.headline: Turkeys 48 cents, eggs 64, valves 98; the Arcade counter closes at noon
columns.body: Dressed turkeys held at 48 cents the pound yesterday at Dutch Kills market, eggs at 64 and cranberries at 11 cents the quart. The Arcade hardware counter closes at noon today with the six-sleeve at 98 cents. The luncheonette asks that the booth telephone not be used for grace.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd's ships coaled at Dunedin. The dogs were walked on the hills. Message concerned coal.

speaker.ear: Fair and cold, high 38, and the whole borough smells of onion. Happy Thanksgiving. One cent, same as ever.

lead.headline: Turkey on the line, and the President-elect on the other one
lead.deck: Two hundred and twelve words from Mr. Hoover at sea, two thousand dinners on Vernon Boulevard, and the elevated stops for once
lead.body: Mr. Hoover sent 212 words from a battleship in the Pacific this morning about gratitude and the harvest, and the Record will play them to Jackson Avenue at noon. We shall be at the Vernon Boulevard hall, where the Legion and the Army feed two thousand from noon. The elevated is on Sunday hours and will stop at the Plaza. Be thankful. The hum is 41, the valve is 98, the ice is five inches and the Speaker is a cent. Not everything went up.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: grace at the Feeneys', heard through the pantry hatch
columns.body: The Alderman says grace at 1:30 and the Lady has it from the hatch that it ran four minutes and mentioned the committee. The new son-in-law said amen a half-second late, which in that house is a position. Everyone cried at the right places.

columns.headline: Dutchman gets an apple and the day off; the ice field gets neither
columns.body: The horse who walked home is in the Vernon Avenue yard today with an apple from Mr. Keller and nothing to haul, and has not looked at the Sound once. The ice field is closed, 1,120 tons in five days and no horse missing, the company reports.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Try the stuffing; everything else in Queens is in it
columns.body: No sightings this week. A man from Ravenswood says he heard it once in August in the small hours, playing a waltz, and went back to sleep. We asked why he did not report it. He said he thought everyone could hear it. Sir, that is the point.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The dogs were walked on the hills at Dunedin and the coal is fine. We are thankful for the dogs.

record.ear: Clear and very cold. High 29. Low 18 at 7 a.m.; the second hard frost. Pipes again.

lead.headline: Board's list unsealed: nine in the counting room at 10:31, one a lineman
lead.deck: Justice Rourke opens the list on Mr. Gorman's motion; eight clerks and a New York Telephone lineman 'present to repair an instrument'; lineman to be found
lead.body: Justice Rourke unsealed the Board of Elections' list yesterday at 2:15 on Mr. Gorman's motion. The list names nine persons present in the Jamaica counting room at 10:31 on the night of the 6th: eight receiving clerks, Mr. Pruitt among them, and one lineman of the New York Telephone Company, 'present to repair an instrument,' whose name the Board did not record. The Board is directed to obtain the name from the company by Monday. The hearing of December 3 stands.

columns.headline: Newtown beats Flushing 13 to 0 before 6,200; Athletic Club and Bayonne draw
columns.body: Newtown High School beat Flushing 13 to 0 at Dutch Kills yesterday morning before 6,200, and the Long Island City Athletic Club drew 7 to 7 with the Bayonne Pioneers in the afternoon before 4,100. Both records were kept. No ruling was disputed.

columns.headline: Mr. Hoover's message played to 400 at noon; crowd stood for 212 words
columns.body: The President-elect's Thanksgiving message was played twice in the Record's window at noon yesterday to a crowd the police put at 400, which stood bareheaded in 36 degrees for its 212 words. The record was clear except for a passage the Navy lays to the Maryland's own engines.

columns.headline: Sunday: elevated stops at the Plaza from 6 a.m.; 180 record an ordinary day
columns.body: The Interborough's Sunday morning stop at Queensboro Plaza begins on Sunday from 6 a.m., and the Phonautograph Society's 180 members will record the same day from waking to sleep for Borough Hall and 1978. The Society asks the Interborough to stop quietly. The company has not replied.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Valves 6 for 99 cents at the Arcade counter; eggs 64; coal 15 dollars. Byrd sails Sunday.

speaker.ear: Eighteen degrees at seven, and the pipes have started talking again. High 29.

lead.headline: Nine in the room at 10:31, and one of them came to fix the telephone
lead.deck: The Board's list is open: eight clerks and a lineman nobody wrote down; the Board has till Monday to find out who he was
lead.body: The list came open at a quarter past two and there were nine names on it. Eight clerks, Mr. Pruitt among them, and a lineman from the telephone company who was in the counting room at 10:31 to repair an instrument, and whom nobody wrote down. Riverhead came in a second time by telephone at 10:31. We do not say the lineman answered it. We say he was standing next to it with a screwdriver. The Board has till Monday to learn his name.

columns.headline: Newtown 13, Flushing nil, and not one word from the record; Club holds Bayonne
columns.body: Six thousand two hundred saw Newtown finish its season without a dispute, so the ground's record went home unplayed, the way records should. The Athletic Club drew seven apiece with Bayonne in the afternoon, which squares last month. Nobody protested anything. We put it down to the turkey.

columns.headline: Four hundred stand in the cold for Mr. Hoover, and the battleship joins in
columns.body: The Record played Mr. Hoover twice at noon and four hundred people stood bareheaded in 36 degrees for 212 words about the harvest, with the Maryland's engines coming through under them like a second opinion. The Navy says engines. We have heard the hum under better speeches than that.

columns.headline: Sunday the elevated stops and the Society records it; 1978 gets the brakes
columns.body: From six on Sunday the Plaza is a stop, and on Sunday a hundred and eighty members of the Phonautograph Society are recording their ordinary day for 1978, so the first thing the future hears from Queens will be the Interborough putting its brakes on.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Valves ninety-nine. Coal fifteen dollars. Byrd sails Sunday. The lineman has till Monday, and so does the Board.
